script.title: Getting a mortgage as a freelancer: what lenders see on your tax return
script.hook: If you freelance and you're thinking about buying a home, the mortgage process works a little differently for you. There are no pay stubs to hand over. Instead, the lender reads your tax returns, and the number they care about isn't the one you probably think. In this video we'll follow one fictional freelancer through how a lender counts self-employed income, the documents you'll be asked for, the trade-off between write-offs and loan size, and what to do in the year or two before you apply. This is education, not lending or tax advice, and every lender has its own rules, so ask yours.

segments.heading: Intro

Instead, the lender reads your tax returns, and the number they care about isn't the one you probably think. In this video we'll follow one fictional freelancer through how a lender counts self-employed income, the documents you'll be asked for, the trade-off between write-offs and loan size, and what to do in the year or two before you apply. This is education, not lending or tax advice, and every lender has its own rules, so ask yours.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding a small house and a folder. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Alex
segments.narration: Meet Alex, a fictional freelance designer. Alex has freelanced full-time for three years. Last year, twenty twenty-six, Alex billed eighty-five thousand dollars. After software, equipment, a home office and other business costs, Schedule C shows sixty-two thousand dollars of profit. The year before, twenty twenty-five, profit was forty-eight thousand. Alex wants to apply for a mortgage this fall.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes next to a laptop and two coin stacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: History
segments.narration: First, history. Many lenders want to see two years of self-employment. Some loan programs accept one year if you worked in the same field as an employee before, but two years of returns is the common starting point. If you went freelance six months ago, you may need to wait, or apply with a co-borrower's income. Alex has three years, so this part is fine.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with two years marked. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Profit
segments.narration: Second, the number. A lender doesn't use what you billed. It starts from your net profit on Schedule C, line thirty-one. That's revenue minus every expense you deducted. For Alex, that's sixty-two thousand for twenty twenty-six, not eighty-five. This surprises a lot of freelancers, because the bigger number is the one they see in their bank account.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with the bottom line circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Add-backs
segments.narration: Third, some costs come back. A few deductions don't take cash out of your pocket each year, so many lenders add them back. Depreciation is the big one: if Alex deducted a computer over several years, that depreciation is added back. Fannie Mae's cash flow worksheet also adds back the business use of home deduction. Meals and other items may be treated differently. Ask your lender which add-backs they use.
segments.on_screen_text: Some non-cash costs are added back
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin coming back to a stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Average
segments.narration: Fourth, the average. Most lenders average the last two years. Alex had forty-eight thousand, then sixty-two thousand. The average is fifty-five thousand dollars a year, or about four thousand five hundred eighty-three a month. If income went down from one year to the next, a lender may use the lower year, or ask for an explanation. Rising income, like Alex's, is the easy case.

segments.heading: Revenue vs counted
segments.narration: Here's the whole picture side by side. Eighty-five thousand billed. Sixty-two thousand of profit last year, forty-eight the year before. Fifty-five thousand counted for the loan. That's almost thirty thousand dollars less than the number Alex had in mind, and it changes how much house Alex can afford.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four bars of different heights. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Debt to income
segments.narration: Fifth, the ratio. The lender compares your monthly debts, including the new mortgage payment, with that monthly income. Limits depend on the loan, often somewhere in the forty-three to fifty percent range. At four thousand five hundred eighty-three a month, forty-three percent is about one thousand nine hundred seventy dollars for every monthly debt combined: the mortgage, taxes and insurance, a car loan, student loans and card minimums.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pie with a slice marked. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Documents
segments.narration: Sixth, paperwork. Expect to hand over your last two years of personal tax returns with all schedules, recent bank statements, and sometimes a year-to-date profit and loss statement if you're applying well into the year. Many lenders also ask you to sign Form 4506-C so they can pull your transcripts from the IRS and check they match. Some want proof the business exists, like a license or client contracts.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a folder with pages. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Transcripts
segments.narration: Before you apply, download your own transcripts. In your IRS online account, the Get Transcript tool gives you a free tax return transcript for each year. Check that the income and tax match the returns you're handing over. If you filed an amended return, or something looks off, sort it out first, so the lender doesn't find it before you do.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a simple form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Write-offs
segments.narration: Now the trade-off. Every legitimate deduction lowers your tax, and it also lowers the income a lender counts. Say Alex had five thousand dollars more in deductions each year. That might save around eleven hundred dollars of federal income tax a year in the twenty-two percent bracket, but it cuts qualifying income by about four hundred seventeen dollars a month. Neither choice is wrong. Just know both effects before you file.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a seesaw with a coin and a house. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Honesty
segments.narration: One line you never cross: don't leave real income off, and don't invent expenses, in either direction. Lenders compare your returns with IRS transcripts and your bank statements. Overstating income on a loan application is a serious problem, and so is understating it to the IRS. The goal is accurate returns and a plan for timing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield with a checkmark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Taxes owed
segments.narration: Pay your taxes. An unpaid balance with the IRS, or a missing return, can stall an application. If you owe, an installment agreement in good standing may be acceptable to some lenders, but it's simpler to be current. Staying on top of quarterly estimated payments helps here too: you don't arrive at April with a big bill right before closing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin going into a slot. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Year before
segments.narration: If you're a year or two out, here's the prep. File on time every year. Keep business money in its own account, so statements are easy to read. Keep monthly books, so a profit and loss statement takes minutes. Avoid big new debts. Build the down payment and some cash reserves. And talk to a lender early: ask how they'll count your income, and whether a certain loan type fits.
segments.on_screen_text: One year out: the prep list
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a checklist. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Co-borrower
segments.narration: If you're buying with a partner who has W-2 income, the application can include both incomes. That can make a newer freelance business less of an issue. The lender still looks at your returns, but the W-2 income is verified with pay stubs and a W-2. Ask how each income will be counted before you assume.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coin stacks, one with a paycheck. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Other loans
segments.narration: There are also non-traditional loans for self-employed borrowers, sometimes called bank statement loans, that use deposits instead of tax returns. They can help in some situations, but they often have higher rates or larger down payments. Compare the total cost carefully, and get any offer in writing.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two doors, one with a small price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Reserves
segments.narration: Lenders also look at what's left after closing. Freelancers with uneven income are often asked for cash reserves: a few months of mortgage payments sitting in savings after the down payment and closing costs. Your tax savings account doesn't count as spare money if that tax is still owed, so don't let a lender, or yourself, treat it as a cushion.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with a small house on the lid. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Timeline
segments.narration: A simple timeline. Two years out: file on time, separate your accounts, keep monthly books. One year out: talk to a lender, check your credit report, and decide whether you'll take any optional deductions. A few months out: download your transcripts, prepare a year-to-date profit and loss statement, and avoid new debts or big business purchases on credit until you close.

segments.heading: Questions
segments.narration: Three questions worth asking any lender up front. How will you count my self-employment income, and which add-backs do you use? Do you need a year-to-date profit and loss statement, and does it need to be prepared by a tax professional? And which loan types fit someone with my history? The answers tell you quickly whether a lender works with freelancers often.

segments.narration: Recap. Lenders usually want two years of self-employment. They start from Schedule C profit, not revenue, add back some non-cash costs, and average two years. That monthly number is measured against all your debts. Bring returns, statements, maybe a profit and loss statement, and expect Form 4506-C. script.title: Foreign clients and working abroad: how a US freelancer's taxes work
script.hook: More freelancers than ever have a client in another country, and some of us think about working from abroad for a few months or a few years. The US tax rules for both are simpler than people fear, but there are a few traps. In this video: how to report payments from foreign clients, converting currencies, the forms that confuse people, and what actually changes if you move abroad, with one fictional freelancer's numbers. Education, not tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: More freelancers than ever have a client in another country, and some of us think about working from abroad for a few months or a few years. The US tax rules for both are simpler than people fear, but there are a few traps. In this video: how to report payments from foreign clients, converting currencies, the forms that confuse people, and what actually changes if you move abroad, with one fictional freelancer's numbers. Education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a globe and a laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Priya
segments.narration: Meet Priya, a fictional freelance developer living in the US. She expects sixty thousand dollars of profit this year. About half comes from clients in the UK and Germany, paid in pounds and euros. The other half is from US clients. She's also wondering about spending next year in Portugal.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a laptop and two small flags as simple shapes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Taxed the same
segments.narration: Rule one: if you're a US citizen or resident, the US taxes your worldwide income. So Priya's foreign client payments go on Schedule C next to her US clients. There's no separate form for foreign freelance income, and no special rate. It's self-employment tax plus income tax, exactly the same as a domestic payment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a globe stamp. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: No 1099
segments.narration: Rule two: don't wait for a 1099. Foreign clients usually don't send one, because 1099 rules are for US payers. That doesn't change anything. You report what you were paid. Your own records, invoices and bank deposits are the source. If you were paid through a US payment platform, you might get a 1099-K for some of it, and that's fine too: just don't count anything twice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an empty mailbox. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Dollars
segments.narration: Rule three: everything goes on your return in US dollars. When you're paid in a foreign currency, you generally use the exchange rate on the day you received it. The IRS also publishes yearly average exchange rates, which some people use for regular payments. Whatever you choose, use it the same way all year and write it down.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coins with different symbols. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Example
segments.narration: Example, with a made-up rate. A German client pays Priya two thousand euros. On that day, one euro is one dollar ten. That's two thousand two hundred dollars of income. Her payment app keeps forty dollars in fees and conversion costs, so two thousand one hundred sixty lands in her account. She reports two thousand two hundred as income and deducts the forty as a business expense.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin turning into another coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Forms
segments.narration: Rule four: the forms. A foreign client may send you a W-8BEN. That form is for foreign people telling a US payer they're not US taxpayers. Priya is a US person, so it's the wrong form. If a client needs her tax status, she can give a W-9, ideally with an EIN rather than her Social Security number. Some countries have their own forms for withholding. If a client withholds foreign tax, keep the paperwork, because a foreign tax credit may apply.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two forms, one crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Quarterlies
segments.narration: Rule five: include it in your estimated taxes. Priya's foreign income is half her profit, so it's half the reason she owes quarterly payments. At sixty thousand of profit, her federal tax is about twelve thousand thirty-seven, or about three thousand nine a quarter. Foreign income often arrives in bigger, irregular chunks, so set aside a share of every payment as it lands.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four calendar pages. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Accounts
segments.narration: Rule six: foreign bank accounts. If Priya opens an account abroad, and the total in all her foreign accounts goes over ten thousand dollars at any point in the year, she generally must file an FBAR, FinCEN Form one fourteen. It's a report, not a tax, filed online, due April fifteenth with an automatic extension to October fifteenth. Penalties for skipping it can be large.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three jars with a line. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Moving abroad
segments.narration: Now Portugal. If Priya moves abroad, she still files a US tax return every year, because the US taxes its citizens wherever they live. What changes is that she may qualify for the foreign earned income exclusion. To qualify, she needs a tax home abroad and either bona fide residence in another country for a full tax year, or physical presence abroad for three hundred thirty full days in twelve months.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a suitcase and a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The exclusion
segments.narration: The exclusion can remove earned income, up to an annual limit the IRS sets, from US income tax. You claim it on Form twenty-five fifty-five. For Priya, at sixty thousand of profit and no other income, it could bring her US income tax to zero. But there's a catch, and it's the one that surprises people.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: SE tax stays
segments.narration: The exclusion doesn't apply to self-employment tax. Priya would still owe US self-employment tax on her net earnings: about eight thousand four hundred seventy-eight dollars. So instead of twelve thousand thirty-seven living in the US, it's about eight thousand four hundred seventy-eight living abroad, before any tax her new country charges.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack still standing. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Comparison
segments.narration: Here it is side by side. Living in the US with sixty thousand of profit: about twelve thousand thirty-seven federal. Living abroad with the exclusion and no foreign social tax: about eight thousand four hundred seventy-eight, all of it self-employment tax. The country she moves to will usually tax her too, and that's the real cost to compare.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two bars side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: Federal tax on $60K of profit
chart.note: 2026 federal, single. No totalization agreement. Before foreign tax.

segments.heading: Agreements
segments.narration: There's one exception for self-employment tax. The US has Social Security agreements, called totalization agreements, with a few dozen countries. Under them, a self-employed person usually pays into the social system of the country where they live, not both. If Priya's new country has one, she may get a certificate showing she's covered there, and stop owing US self-employment tax. The Social Security Administration lists the countries.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two flags as simple shapes. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Credit option
segments.narration: Instead of the exclusion, some people use the foreign tax credit, which reduces US income tax by the income tax paid to another country. Which one is better depends on the other country's rates. In a high-tax country, the credit can work better. This is the point where a cross-border tax preparer is worth paying for.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a fork in a path. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deadlines
segments.narration: Two deadline notes for abroad. US citizens living abroad get an automatic two-month extension to file, to June fifteenth, but interest still runs on any tax owed after April fifteenth. And estimated payments are still due on the usual dates, because self-employment tax doesn't go away.
segments.on_screen_text: Abroad: file by Jun 15, pay by Apr 15
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with two dates. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State tax
segments.narration: Don't forget your state. If you live in a state with an income tax, it generally taxes your freelance income wherever your clients are, just like the IRS. If you move abroad, some states keep treating you as a resident unless you clearly cut ties, such as selling or renting out your home there and changing your driver's license. Check your state's residency rules before you go.
segments.on_screen_text: Your state may still tax you
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map outline with a small plane. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: Keep a simple log for foreign payments: date received, the amount in the foreign currency, the exchange rate and where you got it, the dollar amount, and any fees. If you live abroad, also keep a travel calendar with the days you were in and out of the US, because the physical presence test counts full days. Those two records answer most questions later.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a notebook and a small calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Contracts
segments.narration: One practical tip for foreign clients: put the currency in the contract. Invoice in dollars if you want the client to carry the exchange risk, or in their currency if that wins you the work, and price in a small buffer. Either way, the tax rules don't change. What you report is the dollar value of what you actually received.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Living in the US, foreign client payments are ordinary Schedule C income, reported in US dollars, with or without a 1099. Deduct the fees, give a W-9 not a W-8BEN, and include it in your quarterlies. Foreign accounts over ten thousand dollars mean an FBAR. Moving abroad, you still file, the exclusion can remove income tax but not self-employment tax, and a totalization agreement may change that. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

script.title: Roth IRA or traditional IRA? Three freelancers, real numbers
script.hook: Every freelancer who opens an IRA hits the same question: Roth or traditional? The usual answer, it depends on your tax bracket, is true but not very useful. In this video we'll put real twenty twenty-six numbers on it for three fictional freelancers, show why a traditional IRA deduction is often worth less to a freelancer than you'd expect, and cover the rules that make a Roth more flexible. Education, not advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Every freelancer who opens an IRA hits the same question: Roth or traditional? The usual answer, it depends on your tax bracket, is true but not very useful. In this video we'll put real twenty twenty-six numbers on it for three fictional freelancers, show why a traditional IRA deduction is often worth less to a freelancer than you'd expect, and cover the rules that make a Roth more flexible. Education, not advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding two piggy banks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The basics
segments.narration: Both accounts have the same yearly limit. For twenty twenty-six that's seven thousand five hundred dollars, or more if you're fifty or older. Twenty twenty-seven's limit may be higher, so check irs.gov. A traditional IRA can give you a deduction now, and you pay income tax when you take money out in retirement. A Roth gives no deduction now, but qualified withdrawals later are tax-free, growth included.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two equal piggy banks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Compensation
segments.narration: You need earned income to contribute, and for a freelancer that's your net earnings from self-employment, minus half your self-employment tax. If you contribute to a SEP or Solo 401(k), those contributions come off too. Most freelancers with a few thousand dollars of profit or more clear that easily.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a small slice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Three
segments.narration: Meet three fictional freelancers, all single, no other income. Mia, in her first year, expects thirty-five thousand of profit. Dev expects sixty thousand. Rosa expects a hundred thousand. Each is thinking about putting seventy-five hundred dollars into an IRA. The question is how much a traditional IRA would save each of them in federal tax this year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three coin stacks of different heights. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mia
segments.narration: Mia first. Her federal tax at thirty-five thousand of profit is about six thousand two hundred seventy-four. With a seventy-five hundred dollar traditional IRA deduction, it's about five thousand six hundred sixty. That's a saving of about six hundred fifteen dollars, or eight point two percent of what she put in.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a short coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Dev
segments.narration: Dev next. At sixty thousand, his tax goes from about twelve thousand thirty-seven to about eleven thousand three hundred seventeen. About seven hundred twenty dollars saved, nine point six percent. Not the twelve percent you might expect from his bracket.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a medium coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why less
segments.narration: Here's why. Most freelancers get the twenty percent qualified business income deduction, and it's capped at twenty percent of taxable income before the deduction. When an IRA deduction lowers taxable income, that cap shrinks too. So a dollar of IRA deduction saves your bracket rate times about eighty percent. And the IRA doesn't touch self-employment tax at all.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pie with a slice taken twice. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rosa
segments.narration: Rosa, at a hundred thousand. Her tax goes from about twenty-two thousand three hundred sixty-five to about twenty-one thousand forty-five. About thirteen hundred twenty dollars saved, seventeen point six percent. In the twenty-two percent bracket, the deduction is worth almost twice as much as it is to Dev.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tall coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Chart
segments.narration: Side by side: six hundred fifteen for Mia, seven hundred twenty for Dev, thirteen hundred twenty for Rosa. Same deposit, very different tax savings today. The smaller your saving now, the stronger the case for a Roth, because you're giving up very little to make all the future growth tax-free.

segments.heading: Later
segments.narration: The other side of the decision is your rate in retirement. If you expect to have a lot of taxable income later, from a big traditional 401(k), rental income, or a pension, a Roth looks better. If you expect modest income later, a traditional deduction at a high rate now, like Rosa's, can be the better deal. Nobody knows future tax law, which is one reason some people split contributions.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a seesaw. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Flexible
segments.narration: Roth rules are friendlier in a few ways. You can withdraw what you contributed, not the earnings, at any time without tax or penalty. That makes it a reasonable back-up to an emergency fund for a freelancer with lumpy income. Earnings are tax-free once you're fifty-nine and a half and the account has been open five years, with some exceptions.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin coming out of a jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Income limit
segments.narration: Roth IRAs have an income limit. For twenty twenty-six, single filers start to phase out at a hundred fifty-three thousand of modified adjusted gross income, and married couples filing jointly at two hundred forty-two thousand. All three of our freelancers are under it. Above the limit, people sometimes use a backdoor Roth, which has its own rules worth reading first.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a ladder with a bar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: SEP catch
segments.narration: And a catch for the traditional side. If you have a SEP IRA or Solo 401(k), the IRS treats you as covered by a workplace plan. Then your traditional IRA deduction phases out at fairly low income: for twenty twenty-six, starting at eighty-one thousand for single filers. So a freelancer with a SEP and good profit often can't deduct a traditional IRA at all, and a Roth IRA is the natural add-on.
segments.on_screen_text: SEP or Solo 401(k)? IRA deduction may phase out
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small warning sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Solo Roth
segments.narration: If you want bigger Roth savings, many Solo 401(k) plans let you make Roth employee deferrals, up to twenty-four thousand five hundred for twenty twenty-six. The employer part goes in pre-tax. That way a higher-profit freelancer can get a deduction on one part and Roth treatment on the other.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two piggy banks, one taller. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deadline
segments.narration: Timing. You can contribute to an IRA for a tax year until that year's filing deadline, usually mid-April, not December thirty-first. That's useful for freelancers: you can wait until you know the year's profit, then decide. If you pick traditional and later want Roth, you can usually recharacterize a contribution before the deadline too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with April circled. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Growth
segments.narration: Here's why the Roth math can matter more than the deduction. Say, hypothetically, Mia's seventy-five hundred dollars doubles over the years to fifteen thousand. In a Roth, that whole fifteen thousand comes out tax-free in retirement, if the rules are met. In a traditional IRA, the fifteen thousand is taxed as income when it comes out. Mia gave up about six hundred fifteen dollars of tax savings today to avoid that future tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small plant growing out of a piggy bank. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Spouse
segments.narration: Married? A spouse with little or no income can still have their own IRA, funded from the freelancer's earnings, as long as you file jointly and have enough combined earned income. That can double what a couple puts away. The Roth income limit for married couples filing jointly is much higher than for single filers.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two piggy banks side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Three mistakes to avoid. Putting in more than the limit, across all your IRAs combined, or more than your earned income: the excess is charged a six percent tax each year until you fix it. Contributing to a Roth when your income is over the limit. And forgetting to invest the money once it's in the account. A contribution sitting as cash doesn't grow.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Start
segments.narration: If you're stuck, a simple starting point many people use: in a low-profit year, like a first year, put what you can into a Roth IRA. As profit grows, add a SEP or Solo 401(k) for the bigger deduction. You don't have to get it perfect. Each year is a fresh decision, and you can make it at tax time, once you know your numbers.
segments.on_screen_text: Low year: Roth. Growing: add SEP or Solo
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a staircase with piggy banks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Taxes now
segments.narration: One more thing a Roth doesn't change: your quarterly payments. Because there's no deduction, a Roth contribution doesn't lower this year's tax at all. A traditional IRA contribution does, so if you're sure you'll make one, you can include it when you work out your estimated payments. If you're not sure, leave it out and enjoy a slightly smaller April bill.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four calendar pages with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. Same limit, opposite timing: traditional saves tax now, Roth saves it later. For freelancers, the business income deduction makes a traditional IRA worth less than the bracket suggests: about six hundred fifteen dollars at thirty-five thousand, seven hundred twenty at sixty, thirteen hundred twenty at a hundred, on a seventy-five hundred dollar deposit. Low saving now points to a Roth. Watch the Roth income limit, and the IRA deduction phase-out if you have a SEP or Solo 401(k). Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

script.title: The September 15 tax payment, worked out for three freelancers
script.hook: September fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven, is the third estimated tax payment of the year. It's the one freelancers forget most, because it lands right after summer. In this video we'll cover what this payment is for, the two ways to work out the amount, three fictional freelancers' numbers, what to do if you missed June, and how to schedule it today so you don't have to remember. Twenty twenty-six federal figures, education not advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: September fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven, is the third estimated tax payment of the year. It's the one freelancers forget most, because it lands right after summer. In this video we'll cover what this payment is for, the two ways to work out the amount, three fictional freelancers' numbers, what to do if you missed June, and how to schedule it today so you don't have to remember. Twenty twenty-six federal figures, education not advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a calendar page. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Who
segments.narration: Who needs to pay? If you expect to owe a thousand dollars or more in federal tax for the year after withholding and credits, you're expected to make estimated payments. For most full-time freelancers that's anyone with more than about seven thousand dollars of profit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin with a small flag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Period
segments.narration: The September payment covers income from June first through August thirty-first. The four periods aren't equal: three months, two months, three months, then four. September's payment is due Wednesday, September fifteenth. The next one after it is in January. Because January fifteenth, twenty twenty-eight, is a Saturday and the seventeenth is Martin Luther King Jr. Day, it should fall on Tuesday, January eighteenth.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four calendar blocks of different widths. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Two methods
segments.narration: There are two common ways to work out the amount. Method one: last year's tax. Pay a quarter of your total twenty twenty-six tax each time, or a hundred ten percent of it if your adjusted gross income was over a hundred fifty thousand. Method two: this year's tax. Project this year's profit, work out the tax, and pay a quarter of at least ninety percent of it. You avoid a penalty if you meet either one.
segments.on_screen_text: Last year's tax or this year's
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two arrows into one jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Which
segments.narration: Method one is the simplest and penalty-proof, even if your income grows. The downside: if this year is much bigger, you'll owe the difference in April. Method two follows your real income, which helps in a down year. Many freelancers use last year as the floor and save extra in their tax account if the year is running hot.
segments.on_screen_text: Floor: last year. Save extra if up
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a jar with a line drawn higher. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Kai
segments.narration: Now three fictional freelancers using method two, all single with no other income. First, Kai, expecting forty thousand of profit this year. Self-employment tax is about five thousand six hundred fifty-two. Income tax, after the standard deduction and the business income deduction, about seventeen seventy-five. Total about seven thousand four hundred twenty-seven. A quarter is about eighteen hundred fifty-seven.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a short coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Lena
segments.narration: Second, Lena, at seventy-five thousand. Self-employment tax about ten thousand five hundred ninety-seven, income tax about four thousand eight hundred ninety-eight. Total about fifteen thousand four hundred ninety-five. A quarter is about three thousand eight hundred seventy-four.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a medium coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Omar
segments.narration: Third, Omar, at a hundred twenty thousand. Self-employment tax about sixteen thousand nine hundred fifty-five, income tax about eleven thousand five hundred six. Total about twenty-eight thousand four hundred sixty-two. A quarter is about seven thousand one hundred fifteen. Notice the share of profit going to federal tax: eighteen point six percent for Kai, twenty point seven for Lena, twenty-three point seven for Omar.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tall coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Side by side
segments.narration: Side by side, the September fifteenth payment: about eighteen fifty-seven for Kai, thirty-eight seventy-four for Lena, seventy-one fifteen for Omar. Add your state's estimated payment on top if your state has an income tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three bars rising. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Re-project
segments.narration: If you're using this year's numbers, re-project before you pay. Take your profit from January through August, multiply by twelve, divide by eight. If summer was slow and you expect less, your payment can drop. If you landed a big client, it should go up. Using last year's tax instead? Nothing to re-project. Just pay the same quarter.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a dotted coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Missed June
segments.narration: Missed June fifteenth? Pay it now, not in September. The penalty works like interest, figured separately for each payment, for the days it's late. Example: if Lena's thirty-eight seventy-four went in on September fifteenth instead of June fifteenth, ninety-two days late, at an annual rate of seven percent, that's about sixty-eight dollars. Paying sooner cuts it. The IRS sets the rate each quarter.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a clock next to a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Uneven
segments.narration: If most of your income came late in the year, or one big project landed in August, the annualized income method can lower the earlier payments' penalties. You show when you actually earned the money on Schedule AI of Form twenty-two ten when you file. It takes more work, but it can help freelancers with lumpy income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a chart with a late spike. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pay
segments.narration: To pay, IRS Direct Pay is free from a bank account. Choose estimated tax, form ten forty ES, and tax year twenty twenty-seven. Be careful with that year: picking the wrong one is a common mistake. You can also pay through your IRS online account, or EFTPS. Card payments go through processors that charge a fee.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with three dropdowns. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Schedule
segments.narration: You can schedule the payment ahead of time. Direct Pay lets you pick a future date, up to a year out, and you can change or cancel it up to two business days before. If you know your amount today, schedule September fifteenth now and save the confirmation number. Then do the same for January fifteenth.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with a checkmark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: After
segments.narration: After you pay, write the amount and date in your records, and move the same amount out of your tax savings so your balance shows what's still owed. Then check one more number: your tax savings percentage. If you're paying more than you saved, raise the percentage for the rest of the year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a notebook and a jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Most states with an income tax also want estimated payments, usually on the same dates as the IRS, though a few differ. The state amount is smaller, often a few percent of profit, but the penalty works the same way. Look up your state revenue department's estimated payment page and schedule it at the same time as the federal one.
segments.on_screen_text: Your state: often the same dates
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map outline with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Married
segments.narration: Married and filing jointly? You can make joint estimated payments covering both of you, and the safe harbor is based on your joint tax. If one of you has a W-2 job, extra withholding from that paycheck can cover the freelance tax instead. Withholding counts as paid evenly through the year, so it can even make up for a missed June payment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two rings and a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Four mistakes with the September payment. Picking tax year twenty twenty-six instead of twenty twenty-seven in Direct Pay. Paying from the business account without logging it. Skipping it because summer was slow, without re-projecting. And spending the tax savings over the summer, then finding the account short in September.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four small warning signs. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Ahead
segments.narration: Looking ahead: after September, only one payment is left for twenty twenty-seven, due Tuesday, January eighteenth, twenty twenty-eight, covering September through December. That's also when holiday spending and slow client payments collide, so start the January fund now. The free calendar and calculator in the link in bio show both dates and the amounts.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with one more date. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Day job
segments.narration: If you also have a W-2 job, you have the same withholding option yourself. Give your employer a new Form W-4 with an extra amount per paycheck in step four c. With about nine biweekly paychecks left in the year after mid-August, dividing what you'd owe for September and January by nine gives a rough per-paycheck figure. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator works out a more precise number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a paycheck with a plus sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Set-aside
segments.narration: And check your set-aside percentage against these numbers. Kai's tax is about eighteen point six percent of profit, Lena's about twenty point seven, Omar's twenty-three point seven, before state tax. If you've been saving fifteen percent at Omar's level, September is when you'll feel it. Raising the percentage now spreads the catch-up over the rest of the year instead of landing it all in April.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three jars with lines at different heights. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap. September fifteenth covers June through August. Pay a quarter of last year's tax, a hundred ten percent if your AGI was over a hundred fifty thousand, or a quarter of at least ninety percent of this year's. For our three freelancers: about eighteen fifty-seven, thirty-eight seventy-four and seventy-one fifteen. Missed June? Pay it now. Schedule the payment in Direct Pay with tax year twenty twenty-seven, then log it. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.
